candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — infusion-related adverse reactions
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize the characteristic infusion-related flushing and pruritus associated with rapid IV vancomycin administration and distinguish it from an unsupported diagnosis of definite IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.

options.A: Recognize an infusion-related vancomycin reaction associated with rapid administration, including upper-body flushing and pruritus.
options.B: Recognize definite IgE-mediated anaphylaxis solely from the flushing pattern even though the airway and blood pressure remain stable.
options.C: Interpret the flushing as evidence of inadequate vancomycin exposure and increase the infusion because this reaction indicates underdosing.
options.D: Interpret the rash as unrelated to vancomycin because rapid infusion is not associated with flushing or pruritic skin findings.

candidate.rationale: Current vancomycin labeling describes infusion-related events during or soon after rapid IV administration, including pruritus or urticaria and upper-body flushing. With stable blood pressure and airway, these findings support an infusion-related vancomycin reaction; they do not by themselves establish definite IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. Therefore A is correct. C misinterprets the reaction as underdosing, and D contradicts the labeled adverse-reaction profile.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Rapid IV vancomycin can cause an infusion-related reaction with upper-body flushing and pruritus; those findings alone do not prove definite IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.

candidate.stem: A client develops upper-body flushing and pruritus during a rapid vancomycin infusion while blood pressure and airway remain stable. What is the best interpretation?
